'''Johanna Rommens''' is a Canadian geneticist who was on the research team which identified and cloned the [[Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator|CFTR gene]], which when mutated, is responsible for causing [[cystic fibrosis]] (CF). She later discovered the gene responsible for [[Shwachman–Diamond syndrome|Shwachman-Diamond syndrome]], a rare genetic disorder that causes [[Pancreas|pancreatic]] and [[Hematology|hematologic]] problems.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Sick Kids researchers identify gene for Shwachman-Diamond syndrome|url=http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2002-12/uot-skr122002.php|access-date=2021-01-09|website=EurekAlert!|language=en}}</ref> She is a Senior Scientist Emeritus at [[The Hospital for Sick Children (Toronto)|SickKids]] Research Institute and a professor in the Department of Molecular Genetics at the [[University of Toronto]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|last=uoftmedgen|date=2020-04-17|title=Primer Walking to Personal Medicine: A shift in Medical Genomics|url=https://uoftmedicalgenomics.home.blog/2020/04/17/primer-walking-to-personal-medicine-a-shift-in-medical-genomics/|access-date=2021-01-09|website=The MedGen Project|language=en}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Rommens grew up on a farm in eastern [[New Brunswick]], Canada.<ref name=":4" /> She earned both her bachelor's degree and a PhD in molecular biology from the [[University of New Brunswick]] in [[Fredericton]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|title=Lifeside up {{!}} UNB|url=https://www.unb.ca/difference/rommens.html|access-date=2021-01-09|website=www.unb.ca}}</ref> She was awarded a Beaverbrook Scholarship for her undergraduate education,<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=Celebrating 100 years of Beaverbrook Scholars|url=https://www.unb.ca/giving/impact/scholarships/beaverbrook/award.html|access-date=2021-01-16|website=www.unb.ca}}</ref> and she earned a dual undergraduate degree in biology and organic chemistry.<ref name=":3" /> During her graduate education she studied synthetic chemistry in addition to molecular biology, and she received her PhD in 1986.<ref name=":4" /> In 1986, she started post-doctoral training in the lab of [[Lap-Chee Tsui]] at [[The Hospital for Sick Children (Toronto)|the Hospital for Sick Children]] in [[Toronto|Toronto, Canada]] (commonly referred to as SickKids).<ref name=":52"/>

== Career ==
Rommens became a senior scientist at [[The Hospital for Sick Children (Toronto)|the Hospital for Sick Children]] in Toronto, Canada and a professor at the [[University of Toronto]].<ref name=":3" />

== Research ==

Rommens helped identify the gene behind [[cystic fibrosis]], the [[Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator|CFTR gene]] (short for cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator), which was found to be an ion channel. This work was carried out when she was a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of [[Lap-Chee Tsui]] at the [[The Hospital for Sick Children (Toronto)|Hospital for Sick Children]] (SickKids) in Toronto, Canada, and was a collaboration between Tsui's lab, including fellow postdoctoral researcher [[Batsheva Kerem]], and a team of researchers led by [[Francis Collins]] at the [[University of Michigan]].<ref name=":42">{{Cite journal|last=Marx|first=J. L.|date=1989-09-01|title=The cystic fibrosis gene is found|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.2772644|journal=Science|language=en|volume=245|issue=4921|pages=923–925|doi=10.1126/science.2772644|issn=0036-8075|pmid=2772644|bibcode=1989Sci...245..923M |url-access=subscription}}</ref> The CFTR gene was discovered through genetic linkage analysis involving looking for genetic markers that were present in patients with cystic fibrosis but not present in their non-affected relatives. Due to the phenomenon of [[Genetic recombination|recombination]], whereby parts of [[chromosome]]s swap homologous segments during [[germ cell]] development, each chromosome a child inherits is a mix of the both of that parent's copies of that chromosome. Markers would only be consistently co-inherited with the gene behind cystic fibrosis if they were close together on the chromosome, so Rommens and other researchers used markers to find the approximate location of the gene.<ref name=":52">{{Cite book|last=Trivedi, Bijal P., 1970-|title=Breath from salt : a deadly genetic disease, a new era in science, and the patients and families who changed medicine forever|year=2020|isbn=978-1-948836-37-1|location=Dallas, TX|oclc=1083824294}}</ref> They then used a combination of chromosome walking and chromosome hopping or jumping to locate the CF gene, which they named cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator ([[Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator|CFTR]]).<ref name=":42" />

Rommens' work on [[cystic fibrosis]] didn't stop after she helped identify the [[Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator|CFTR gene]]. Instead, she continued to research CF once she started her own lab, using her molecular genetics expertise to look outside of the CFTR gene for insight into CF. She helped lead research to discover genetic modifiers of CF - versions of genes other than CFTR that either worsen or ameliorate the effects of CFTR mutations. Such modifiers could help explain why patients with the same CFTR mutations can have differing disease severity.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Moore|first=Charles|title=International Research Consortium Identifies Five Genetic Regions Implicated In Cystic Fibrosis Severity|url=https://cysticfibrosisnewstoday.com/2015/09/30/international-research-consortium-identifies-five-genetic-regions-implicated-cystic-fibrosis-severity/|access-date=2021-01-09|language=en-US}}</ref> For example, around 15 percent of CF patients are born with an intestinal obstruction called [[meconium ileus]], and, by analyzing genomes from almost 4,000 CF patients, Rommens' team found genetic risk factors associated with developing meconium ileus and lung problems.<ref>{{Cite web|title=SickKids-led study identifies multiple genes linked to differences in cystic fibrosis|url=http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2012-04/uot-ssi033112.php|access-date=2021-01-09|website=EurekAlert!|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sun|first1=Lei|last2=Rommens|first2=Johanna M.|last3=Corvol|first3=Harriet|last4=Li|first4=Weili|last5=Li|first5=Xin|last6=Chiang|first6=Theodore A.|last7=Lin|first7=Fan|last8=Dorfman|first8=Ruslan|last9=Busson|first9=Pierre-François|last10=Parekh|first10=Rashmi V.|last11=Zelenika|first11=Diana|date=April 2012|title=Multiple apical plasma membrane constituents are associated with susceptibility to meconium ileus in individuals with cystic fibrosis|journal=Nature Genetics|language=en|volume=44|issue=5|pages=562–569|doi=10.1038/ng.2221|pmid=22466613|issn=1546-1718|pmc=3371103}}</ref> In addition to using genetics to investigate how multiple genes contribute to CF pathology, she used mouse models to study how mutations in the CFTR gene affect multiple organ systems.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Molecular Medicine and Human Genetics|url=http://www.moleculargenetics.utoronto.ca/new-page-3|access-date=2021-01-09|website=Molecular Genetics - University of Toronto|language=en-US|archive-date=2021-01-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210111130801/http://www.moleculargenetics.utoronto.ca/new-page-3|url-status=dead}}</ref>
 
Rommens also investigated the causes of other genetic diseases, chiefly [[Shwachman–Diamond syndrome|Shwachman-Diamond syndrome]] (SDS), a rare [[Dominance (genetics)|autosomal recessive]] genetic disorder that causes [[Pancreas|pancreatic]] and [[Hematology|hematologic]] problems. It presents with some of the same symptoms as CF and, after CF, SDS Is the second most common cause of pancreatic insufficiency in children.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|date=2020-12-08|title=Shwachman-Diamond Syndrome: Practice Essentials, Pathophysiology, Epidemiology|url=https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/958476-overview}}</ref> The pancreas is responsible for producing many [[digestive enzyme]]s and problems with the pancreas in SDS patients prevent sufficient amounts of these enzymes from reaching the intestines, leading to malabsorption of nutrients.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Shwachman Diamond Syndrome|url=https://rarediseases.org/rare-diseases/shwachman-diamond-syndrome/|access-date=2021-01-16|website=NORD (National Organization for Rare Disorders)|language=en-US}}</ref> Among other symptoms, the disease often presents with digestive problems, skeletal abnormalities, and frequent infections.<ref name=":2" /> In 2002, Rommens discovered that SDS is caused by mutations in the [[SBDS|SBDS gene]].<ref name=":1" /> In addition to the SBDS gene, humans have an SBDS [[pseudogene]] (SBDSP), a copy of the SBDS gene which arose via a genetic duplication event, then became inactivated through [[Mutation|genetic mutations]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Whitcomb|first=David C.|date=2003-11-01|title=The genetics of Shwachman-Diamond syndrome|url=https://www.gastrojournal.org/article/S0016-5085(03)01395-7/abstract|journal=Gastroenterology|language=English|volume=125|issue=5|pages=1541–1543|doi=10.1016/j.gastro.2003.04.007|pmid=14598273|issn=0016-5085|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Rommens found that patients with SDS had segments of their normal SBDS genes swapped out for the corresponding (mutated) segments of the pseudogene.<ref name=":1" /> The most common of the mutations they discovered introduced [[Nonsense mutation|premature stop codons]] (PTCs) which led the patients to produce truncated versions of the SBDS protein.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal|last1=Boocock|first1=Graeme R. B.|last2=Morrison|first2=Jodi A.|last3=Popovic|first3=Maja|last4=Richards|first4=Nicole|last5=Ellis|first5=Lynda|last6=Durie|first6=Peter R.|last7=Rommens|first7=Johanna M.|date=January 2003|title=Mutations in SBDS are associated with Shwachman-Diamond syndrome|journal=Nature Genetics|volume=33|issue=1|pages=97–101|doi=10.1038/ng1062|issn=1061-4036|pmid=12496757|s2cid=5091627}}</ref> This gene was uncharacterized at the time, but Rommens' lab and others would go on to show that, among other potential functions, SBDS is involved in ribosomal maturation.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|date=2012-12-16|title=Defective ribosome assembly in Shwachman-Diamond syndrome|url=https://www.fredhutch.org/en/news/spotlight/2012/12/defective-ribosome-assembly-shwachman-diamond-syndrome.html|access-date=2021-01-22|website=Fred Hutch|language=en|archive-date=2021-03-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210307152108/https://www.fredhutch.org/en/news/spotlight/2012/12/defective-ribosome-assembly-shwachman-diamond-syndrome.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Ribosome]]s are cellular protein-making complexes, so problems with SBDS could lead to problems with protein synthesis.<ref name=":6" /> Rommens helped educate families affected with SDS at a weeklong volunteer-run camp called Camp Sunshine in [[Casco, Maine]].<ref name=":4" />

Rommens also discovered genes implicated in breast and prostate cancer, as well as [[Alzheimer's disease]].<ref name=":4" /> She was involved in genetic research on the neurodegenerative disease [[Huntington's disease]] as well as [[Wilson's disease]], a copper storage disorder.<ref name=":5" />
